title: Of the custom of wearing clothes
paragraphs: Whatever I say on this subject, I am bound to trespass on some of the boundaries of custom, so carefully has she sealed off every approach. I was debating with myself, this shivering season, whether the practice of going naked in those nations recently discovered is imposed on them by the heat of the climate — as we say of the Indians and Moors — or whether it is the original fashion of humankind. Men of understanding, since all things under the sun (as Scripture says) are subject to the same laws, used in such cases — where we have to separate the laws of nature from those invented by man — to look to the general order of the world, in which nothing can be counterfeit. Now, since all other creatures are sufficiently furnished with what they need to sustain themselves, it is hardly credible that we alone are brought into the world defective and needy, in a condition that cannot survive without outside help. So I believe that, just as plants, trees, and animals — everything that has life — are seen to be by nature sufficiently clothed and covered to protect them against the weather:
"Proptereaque fere res omnes aut corio sunt, Aut seta, aut conchis, aut callo, aut cortice tectae,"
["And for this reason almost all things are clothed with skin, or hair, or shells, or hide, or bark." — Lucretius, iv. 936.]

so were we; but, like people who put out the day's light by burning artificial light, we have, with borrowed forms and fashions, destroyed our own. And it is plain that custom alone makes impossible what is otherwise not so at all. For of those peoples who know nothing of clothing, some live in the same temperatures we do, and some in much colder climates. Besides, our most tender parts are always exposed to the air — the eyes, mouth, nose, ears — and our country labourers, like our ancestors in earlier times, go with their chests and bellies open. Had we been born with a built-in need for skirts and breeches, no doubt nature would have armoured the parts she meant to expose to the seasons with a thicker skin, as she has done at the fingertips and the soles of the feet. And why should this seem hard to believe? I notice much more distance between my own dress and that of one of our country labourers than between his and that of a man who has no other covering but his skin. How many men, especially in Turkey, go naked out of devotion? Someone asked a beggar, whom he saw walking around in his shirt in the depth of winter, as cheerful as a man wrapped up to the ears in furs, how he could stand to go like that. "Why, sir," he answered, "you go with your face bare; I am all face." The Italians tell a story of the Duke of Florence's fool. When the duke, warmly wrapped, asked him how he, so thinly clad, could bear the cold the duke himself could barely endure, the fool answered: "Try my recipe — put on all the clothes you own at once, and you'll feel no more cold than I do." King Massinissa, into extreme old age, could never be persuaded to cover his head, no matter how cold, stormy, or rainy the weather; the same is told of the Emperor Severus. Herodotus tells us that in the battles between Egyptians and Persians, both he and others observed that of the bodies left on the field the skulls of the Egyptians were beyond comparison harder than those of the Persians, because the latter had gone with their heads always covered from infancy — first with caps, then with turbans — while the others kept theirs always shaved and bare. King Agesilaus, into a decrepit old age, wore the same clothes in winter that he wore in summer. Caesar, says Suetonius, always marched at the head of his army, usually on foot, bareheaded whether it rained or shone; as much is said of Hannibal:
"Tum vertice nudo, Excipere insanos imbres, coelique ruinam."
["Bareheaded he marched through pelting rain and the sky's worst fury." — Silius Italicus, i. 250.]

A Venetian who has lived for a long time in Pegu, and who has lately come back from there, writes that the men and women of that kingdom, though they cover all their other parts, always go barefoot and even ride that way. And Plato strongly advises, for the health of the whole body, to give the head and feet no clothing other than what nature has provided. The man whom the Poles have elected as their king since ours came back from there — one of the greatest princes of the age — never wears gloves, and whatever the weather, in winter or otherwise, wears no other cap outdoors than he wears at home. I, on the other hand, can't stand to be unbuttoned or untied; my neighbouring labourers would feel themselves in chains if they were laced up like me. Varro thinks that when it was decreed we should be bareheaded in the presence of the gods and the magistrate, it was set up more for the sake of health, to harden us against the weather, than out of any sense of reverence. And since we are now on the subject of cold, and since the French used to wear all sorts of colours — not I, since I rarely wear anything but black or white, in imitation of my father — let us add another story from Captain Martin du Bellay, who reports that on the march to Luxembourg he saw such a great frost that the troops' ration-wine was cut with hatchets and wedges and given out to the soldiers by weight, who carried it away in baskets. And Ovid:
"Nudaque consistunt, formam servantia testae, Vina; nec hausta meri, sed data frusta, bibunt."
["And the wines stand bare, keeping the shape of the cask; they drink not gulps of wine, but lumps handed out to them." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 10, 23.]

At the mouth of Lake Maeotis the frosts are so sharp that on the very same ground where Mithridates' lieutenant had fought the enemy dry-shod and given them a serious defeat, the following summer he won a naval victory over them on the same place. The Romans fought at a real disadvantage in their engagement with the Carthaginians near Piacenza, because they went into battle with their blood congealed and their limbs numbed by the cold, while Hannibal had had great fires distributed through his camp to warm his soldiers, and oil given out so that, by rubbing themselves down, they could make their muscles more supple and active and fortify their pores against the violence of the air and freezing wind that raged that season.

The retreat the Greeks made from Babylon back to their own country is famous for the hardships and disasters they had to overcome. One of these: caught in the mountains of Armenia by a terrible snowstorm, they lost all sense of the country and of the roads, and once driven up there spent a day and a night without food or drink. Most of their cattle died, many of the men starved, several were struck blind by the force of the hail and the glare of the snow, many lost fingers and toes, and many were left stiff and motionless by the extreme cold — though still with their minds intact.
Alexander saw a nation where they bury their fruit trees in winter to protect them from being destroyed by the frost, and we ourselves can see the same.

As for clothing, the King of Mexico changed his outfit four times a day and never put the same one on again, using whatever he laid aside in continual gifts and rewards. And no pot, dish, or other utensil from his kitchen or table was ever served twice.
